stories.title: NASA and IBM open-source an AI model for mapping the Moon
stories.summary: NASA and IBM released a free Lunar Foundation Model trained on Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter data and more. Hosted on Hugging Face with open code, it helps scientists map craters, hunt for polar ice, and study old volcanic features without building a model from scratch.
stories.summaryLong:
NASA is bringing artificial intelligence to the study of the Moon, helping researchers transform how they analyze the Moon’s surface. In an ongoing collaboration with IBM Research and several academic institutions, NASA has launched the NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model, among the first open-source AI models built specifically for lunar science. The model, trained primarily on data from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), is hosted publicly on Hugging Face for anyone to use, with the complete codebase available on GitHub for testing and experimentation.

The NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model supports the next generation of lunar science by helping researchers quickly analyze vast quantities of data to better understand the Moon’s surface. Using the model as a mapping tool, researchers can rapidly develop actionable strategies for evaluating the Moon’s rugged surface, understanding its geological past, and planning future lunar research.

“NASA has spent decades building an extraordinary scientific record of the Moon, but collecting data is only part of the job,” said Kevin Murphy, chief science data officer and acting chief data and AI officer at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “We also have to make data easier for scientists to explore and use. The NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model shows what’s possible when we bring AI to NASA’s petabytes of scientific data. That’s a real opportunity we see with AI: turning large-scale data into new discoveries.”

Unlike traditional models that require building and training specialized algorithms from scratch for specific tasks, foundation models are pre-trained on vast, unlabeled datasets. The broad knowledge they acquire through pre-training allows them to generalize across multiple scientific domains through quick fine-tuning.

Data collected by NASA’s LRO over the past 17 years covers most of the lunar surface in detail. The NASA-IBM model was trained on roughly 2 million image tiles from this dataset, comprising more than 1 million high-resolution camera images at 1-meter resolution and nearly 964,000 multispectral images at 100-meter resolution. It also drew on high-resolution Moon imagery and terrain data from missions such as NASA’s GRAIL, NASA’s Lunar Prospector, and JAXA’s Selenological and Engineering Explorer.

Because the foundation model is already pre-trained, planetary scientists can adapt it to many lunar research tasks—mapping craters, spotting young volcanic features, and estimating where ice may exist near the lunar poles—using only small amounts of labeled data. Dark permanently shadowed regions remain cold enough to trap and preserve ice for up to billions of years. Mapping those areas offers insight into the Moon’s history and potential resources for future exploration.

Overall, the model matched or exceeded several strong baseline models across evaluated tasks, with a clear advantage on estimating polar ice stability. Datasets, benchmarks, and integration with the open-source TerraTorch toolkit were released alongside the model so researchers worldwide can build on the work.

stories.title: Thailand eliminates rubella as a public health problem, WHO says
stories.summary: The World Health Organization verified that Thailand has eliminated endemic rubella—the seventh country in WHO’s South-East Asia Region to do so. Years of childhood immunization and careful disease tracking helped protect families from congenital rubella syndrome.
stories.summaryLong:
The World Health Organization today announced that Thailand has been verified for eliminating rubella as a public health problem, marking a major milestone in the country’s efforts to protect children, women and families from vaccine-preventable diseases.

Rubella, also known as German measles, is a contagious viral infection. Rubella infection during pregnancy can cause miscarriage, stillbirth or congenital rubella syndrome, a condition associated with lifelong birth defects. Rubella can be prevented through safe, effective and affordable vaccines.

“Thailand has shown that rubella elimination is achievable when strong political commitment, resilient immunization services, high-quality surveillance and community trust come together. This achievement protects future generations from congenital rubella syndrome and brings the Region closer to eliminating both measles and rubella,” said Dr Nilesh Buddha, Officer-in-Charge, WHO South-East Asia Region, endorsing the recommendation of the Regional Verification Commission for Measles and Rubella Elimination in the South-East Asia Region (SEA-RVC).

The SEA-RVC, which held its annual meeting from 22–23 June 2026, reviewed evidence submitted by Thailand’s National Verification Committee, including data on disease surveillance, molecular epidemiology, immunization coverage, outbreak response and programme performance. This was followed by a verification field visit in July 2026 and the Commission recommended that Thailand be verified for endemic rubella elimination.

Thailand is now the seventh country in the WHO South-East Asia Region to achieve rubella elimination, joining Bhutan, DPR Korea, Maldives, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Timor-Leste. Four countries in the Region - Bhutan, DPR Korea, Maldives and Timor-Leste - have eliminated both measles and rubella.

“This verification is a proud moment for Thailand and a tribute to decades of commitment by our health workers, volunteers, partners and communities. By eliminating rubella, Thailand has protected newborns from preventable lifelong disabilities and reaffirmed its commitment to equitable health services for every child and family. We will sustain this gain and intensify efforts towards measles elimination,” said H.E. Mr Pattana Promphat, Minister of Public Health, Thailand.

Thailand’s Expanded Programme on Immunization was started in 1977 and introduced rubella-containing vaccine into its national immunization programme for girls aged six years in Primary school. in 1986 and expanded it to all children aged one year in 1993. Since then, the country has been strengthening routine immunisation, outbreak response and surveillance systems, supported by strong collaboration between national and subnational health authorities.

The programme emphasized reaching underserved and mobile populations, rapidly investigating suspected measles and rubella cases through fever and rash surveillance, and maintaining laboratory-supported surveillance to detect and respond to any virus transmission.

Verification confirms that Thailand has met the requisite criteria for interruption of endemic rubella virus transmission and has systems in place to sustain this achievement.

stories.title: Bhutan becomes first in its region to eliminate dog-spread rabies
stories.summary: WHO validated Bhutan as the first South-East Asia Region country to eliminate dog-transmitted human rabies as a public health problem. Mass dog vaccination, free bite care, and One Health teamwork kept human deaths at zero since mid-2023.
stories.summaryLong:
The World Health Organization (WHO) has validated Bhutan’s elimination of dog-transmitted rabies as a public health problem in the country. Bhutan is the first country in the WHO South-East Asia Region to achieve this success.

Rabies is a viral disease that is almost always fatal once clinical symptoms appear. However, rabies deaths are preventable. On one hand, vaccinating dogs curbs the disease at its source; on the other, prompt use of post exposure prophylaxis (PEP) stops the virus from reaching the central nervous system after a bite. PEP consists of thorough wound washing, administration of a course of human rabies vaccine and, when indicated, rabies immunoglobulins (RIG) injection.

“I congratulate Bhutan on this historic achievement, which is another step towards our goal to end human deaths from dog-transmitted rabies by 2030,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “Bhutan's success shows that the health of humans, animals and the environment we share is inextricably linked. By uniting health workers, veterinarians, and communities, Bhutan has shown that the fight against rabies is won not in silos, but through solidarity across all sectors."

Bhutan’s achievement is a result of more than a decade of sustained investment in a One Health approach, which recognizes that the health of humans, animals, and ecosystems is closely interlinked. Changes in these relationships can increase the risk of diseases emerging and spreading among both humans and animals. One Health promotes the optimization of human, animal, plant and ecosystem health through coordinated and integrated actions across sectors.

Through this approach, Bhutan has prioritized resource allocation, integrated surveillance, and strategic planning. The approach has proven effective in addressing public health challenges such as rabies. When a suspected rabies case is reported, animal and human health authorities collaborate to identify potential exposures and, when necessary, conduct joint field investigations under the One Health framework.

“Bhutan has shown that eliminating dog-mediated human rabies is possible when strong national leadership, a mature One Health approach and communities come together around a shared goal. The dedication of health workers, veterinary professionals and De-suung volunteers known as ‘Guardians of Peace’ helped take dog vaccination, population management and community awareness to every part of the country. Bhutan’s achievement offers an important example for other countries in the Region,” said Dr Nilesh Buddha, Officer-in-Charge, WHO South-East Asia Region.

stories.title: Western bluebirds return to Vancouver Island after decades
stories.summary: Once declared extinct on Vancouver Island, western bluebirds nested again in the Cowichan Valley this year—30 adults and 126 young—thanks to nest boxes, mealworms, and a cross-border volunteer effort with seventy landowners.
stories.summaryLong:
Seventy years ago, western bluebirds were so common on southern Vancouver Island that their spring return announced the season. As Garry oak meadows were lost to development, the birds vanished. In the mid-1990s they were declared extinct on Vancouver Island and the southern Gulf Islands.

The Cowichan Bring Back the Bluebirds Project has been reversing that loss. This year, a record 30 adult bluebirds nested in the Cowichan Valley and produced 126 young. About 70 private landowners and Cowichan Tribes host nest boxes; volunteers logged roughly 1,000 hours this year and spent about $6,000 on mealworms to encourage extra clutches.

Birds are still brought across the U.S.–Canada border from Joint Base Lewis-McChord near Tacoma, Washington, where prairie habitat still supports healthy bluebird populations. Early June handovers at a gas station near the Peace Arch crossing move families into temporary aviaries before release. Banding already shows Cowichan-born juveniles settling on San Juan Island, and work is underway to seed a Victoria population.

Coordinator Jacquie Taylor told The Tyee the project is about stopping biodiversity loss one species at a time: “We need hands on to make that happen. And we can do it one species at a time.”

stories.title: ESA’s EVE turns Earth satellite data into a conversation
stories.summary: ESA’s Φ-lab showed EVE (Earth Virtual Expert)—a chat-style guide to Earth observation—with humanoid robots Ameca and Frankie that answer plain-language questions about satellite images. The demo aims to make space data approachable for non-specialists.
stories.summaryLong:
Over recent years, ESA Φ-lab and Pi School have built EVE (Earth Virtual Expert), an intelligent companion for exploring Earth observation and Earth sciences, with support from Imperative Space, Mistral AI and Wiley. On 23 September 2026, Φ-lab highlighted how two humanoid robots—Ameca and Frankie, developed by Frank Reply GmbH—make talking to EVE more accessible and engaging.

Earth observation can feel like searching for a needle in a digital haystack. Tracking climate patterns or crop health usually takes specialized expertise. With EVE, people can start with a conversation instead of dense code. Ameca focuses on satellite image searches: speak a plain-language request and it helps locate relevant imagery from EVE’s database. Frankie specializes in vegetation analysis, explaining concepts such as NDVI (Normalised Difference Vegetation Index) while looking at an image on screen.

The robots also offer an interactive image recognition game, an NDVI crop-health inspector, and a “Behind the Scenes” mode that shows retrieval, reasoning, planning, and tool calls as they happen. Daniel Fitzpatrick of Frank Reply said conversational interfaces help democratize Earth observation operations that once required highly specialized knowledge. Nicolas Longépé, EVE’s technical officer at Φ-lab, added that anyone—from curious citizens to policymakers—can ask a question and explore satellite intelligence “just like talking to a friend.”

A demo and hands-on session are planned for the Agentic AI for Earth Observation workshop in Berlin in October, with a fuller public EVE launch expected soon.

stories.title: AI helps find scents that steer bees away from pesticides
stories.summary: UC Riverside researchers used machine learning to screen millions of compounds for bee-safe repellents. Lab and field tests backed top candidates that could keep honey bees off sprayed crops without harming the insects.
stories.summaryLong:
In a win for pollinator conservation, researchers at the University of California, Riverside, have developed a machine learning-based method to identify chemical compounds that can safely repel honey bees from pesticide-treated crops. The research offers a potential solution to one of agriculture’s most urgent ecological challenges: the ongoing decline in honey bee populations, driven in part by pesticide exposure.

The interdisciplinary team led by Anandasankar Ray , a professor of molecular, cell and systems biology and an expert on insect olfactory behavior, tackled a central obstacle in altering behavior of pollinators to protect them: the complexity of the honey bee olfactory system. With more than 200 odor receptors capable of detecting a vast array of volatile compounds, finding scents that repel bees was a major challenge — until now.

“Bees rely heavily on their sense of smell to forage, but that sensitivity makes it tough to find odors that push them away instead of drawing them in,” Ray said. “Our goal was to flip that script and find a way to use scent as a deterrent — safely and effectively.”

To do this, Ray’s team collaborated with honey bee researchers in the lab of Boris Baer , a professor of entomology . The researchers created a machine-learning model trained on both the chemical structures of odorants and previously recorded behavioral responses of bees. The model was refined with new behavioral data the team obtained in the lab from honey bees and Drosophila (fruit flies), allowing for a more accurate prediction of insect olfactory responses. Once optimized, the system screened more than 50 million compounds, ultimately identifying about 130 that were predicted to have strong potential as bee repellents.

“It is generally thought you need abundant data to do any kind of machine learning, but that’s not true for olfaction,” Ray said. “You simply need good-quality data and iterative improvement steps.”

The team reports in the journal eLife how they put the top-performing candidates to the test. In the lab, honey bees exhibited clear avoidance behaviors when exposed to these candidates, aligning closely with the model’s predictions. Subsequent field experiments with freely foraging bees confirmed that all seven compounds tested reliably repelled bees from honey combs without harming them.

“This is a powerful demonstration of how machine learning can help solve real-world ecological problems,” Ray said. “By keeping bees away from harmful pesticides, we can potentially reduce their risk of exposure without compromising the protection of crops.”

A contributing factor to bee population decline and colony collapse likely is unintended exposure to pesticides. While some pesticides that are harmful to bees have been banned or restricted, Ray said there is potential to further lower risks by using the pesticides with repellents that can minimize bee contact.

stories.title: Chinook salmon reclaim most of their historic Klamath range
stories.summary: After the world’s largest dam-removal project on the Klamath River, open-access research finds Chinook salmon already using nearly their full historic freshwater range. Thousands passed the former Iron Gate site in 2024 and 2025.
stories.summaryLong:
In 2024, four hydroelectric dams on the Klamath River were removed in the largest dam-removal project to date, reconnecting habitat that had been blocked for generations of fish. An open-access study in Nature Scientific Reports tracked what happened next for Chinook salmon.

Researchers report that about 7,742 Chinook passed the former Iron Gate site in 2024 and 13,310 in 2025. Within two migratory seasons, fish had reoccupied nearly all of their historic freshwater range in the basin—an unusually fast response after such a large reconnection.

Habitat fragmentation is a major driver of biodiversity loss worldwide, and clear “before and after” evaluations of big restoration projects are still uncommon. The Klamath results give a concrete, public example of how removing barriers can let migratory fish reclaim rivers when water and habitat conditions allow.

The paper’s abstract and results emphasize rapid recolonization rather than a finished recovery story: monitoring continues, and long-term abundance will depend on ocean conditions, water management, and remaining habitat quality. Still, for a river system long symbolized by blocked runs, the early numbers are a rare bright milestone.
stories.summaryLongNote: Verified from the open-access Scientific Reports abstract and results; rewritten for general readers (~220 words).

stories.title: Open-source ORCA turns everyday radios into science radars
stories.summary: CU Boulder’s HI-SNR lab leads ORCA, free software that helps researchers turn commercial software-defined radios into environmental radars for ice, forests, and soils—without proprietary lock-in.
stories.summaryLong:
Radar technology is one of the most powerful tools to better understand our world around us. Researchers use radar to see beneath the surface of ice, forest canopy or soil in ways the human eye never could. As the planet changes, that kind of capability matters more than ever.

Undergraduate researcher, Colin Chow (left), discussing results of radar testing with Assistant Professor Nicole Bienert.

But for the researchers who actually build these tools, there’s a frustrating dilemma: Before a radar system can answer a scientific question, someone has to spend months, oftentimes much longer, building the radar and writing code just to get it operating. It’s a rite of passage familiar to nearly all in the radar research community. A new student joins a lab, inherits a software-defined radio and starts writing the same kind of control code to make it operate as a radar. A team at the University of Colorado Boulder’s High precision Imaging, Signals ‘N Radar (Hi-SNR) Laboratory is working to change that. The lab, based in the Department of Electrical, Computer & Energy Engineering is leading the Open Radar Code Architecture (ORCA) initiative, an open-source software framework that turns commercially available software-defined radios (SRD) into functioning radar systems built specifically for environmental monitoring. “It takes a student a year to get to this base level of radar operation,” said Nicole Bienert, assistant professor of electrical engineering. “Every new student is just recreating the wheel over and over. That’s not an efficient use of our time as researchers if we really want to answer major scientific questions." ORCA is designed to close that gap. Rather than every research group re-writing radar-control code from scratch, ORCA gives them a starting point they can build on, so more radar research questions can get answered.

The project traces its roots to Bienert’s doctoral research in the Stanford Radio Glaciology group and the team she worked with, which included Thomas Teisberg and Anna Broome. ORCA was initially introduced by those researchers for studying the cryosphere, with Teisberg developing a fixed-wing drone system for measuring glacier ice thickness and Broome developing a multi-frequency radar system.

S now levels for avalanche warning. S now water equivalent for water resource management. T ree water content for wildfire risk. Glacier material analysis for sea level rise. Contribute to and connect with ORCA

stories.title: ChatGPT’s phone app can now finish tasks by voice
stories.summary: OpenAI brought voice-based “agentic” features to the ChatGPT mobile app. Plus and Pro users can ask the phone to draft documents, summarize Slack or email, and continue work later on desktop; free users get plugins and connected apps.
stories.summaryLong:
OpenAI announced that it is bringing voice-based agentic features to mobile, allowing users to trigger workflows like drafting documents or summarizing emails from the ChatGPT phone app.

Plus and Pro subscribers can use the Work tab on their phone to create a document, draft an email, or summarize Slack messages. Those users can also build sites, create presentations, use the cloud browser, and reach other Work areas such as finances inside ChatGPT. Free and Go users, meanwhile, can work with plugins and connected apps.

OpenAI said voice conversations will produce richer text output, and users can switch between text and voice more easily. Someone can start a conversation on the go and resume it later on desktop. The company earlier launched conversational model GPT-Live and integrated similar voice task features on desktop; this rollout brings comparable capabilities to mobile.

The update arrives as more people use spoken commands for complex assistant tasks. TechCrunch notes the feature set still keeps chat and workspaces separate, even as competitors experiment with merged interfaces.
stories.summaryLongNote: Verified from TechCrunch’s 23 Sep 2026 report (~180 words; article is short).

stories.title: Endangered water voles return to Surrey’s River Wey
stories.summary: Surrey Wildlife Trust released water voles at Thundry Meadows as part of a community project restoring the species along the River Wey. Soft-release pens for hundreds of voles are now open, and early upstream sites already show feeding signs and burrows.
stories.summaryLong:
Surrey Wildlife Trust announced the introduction of 30 nationally endangered water voles to its Thundry Meadows nature reserve near Elstead on 16 September 2026. The release is part of a wider community effort—led by the National Trust, River Wey Trust and South East Rivers Trust, and funded by the Environment Agency’s Environment Improvement Fund—to bring a locally extinct species back to the River Wey from the South Downs to the Thames.

Following successful releases on the upper Wey, the project moved downstream to ten sites between Frensham and Elstead, including Thundry Meadows and partner estates. About 300 water voles were raised by Derek Gow Consultancy and introduced in soft-release pens with food, water, and shelter; pens have since been removed so animals can disperse at their own pace.

Water voles have been functionally extinct in Surrey since the early 2000s. Sometimes called “miniature beavers,” they reshape wetlands in ways that help wildflowers, insects, birds, and flood-absorbing bank burrows. Early monitoring on the upper Wey already shows feeding signs, burrows, latrines, camera detections, and e-DNA evidence that populations are establishing and expanding.

National Trust lead ranger David Elliott put the partnership simply: “Nature wins when we work together… It’s so encouraging to see the water voles returning after all this time.”

stories.title: Olive ridley turtles nest on the U.S. West Coast for the first time
stories.summary: Responders documented olive ridley turtles nesting near Seal Beach and Huntington Beach—the first known natural sea-turtle nesting on the U.S. West Coast. Scientists link the unusual visits to warm Super El Niño ocean conditions.
stories.summaryLong:
Left: An olive ridley turtle nesting near the Huntington Beach Pier. Right: Eggs laid near Seal Beach. Left: Huntington Beach Fire Department. Right: NOAA Fisheries. Both via Facebook This month, Southern California hosted some very special guests—who left behind historic mementos.

On September 16, an olive ridley turtle dug a nest and laid her eggs near Seal Beach in Orange County. It represents the U.S. West Coast’s first known natural sea turtle nesting, according to a social media post by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Fisheries West Coast. Then, three days later, a sea turtle of the same species was seen doing the same thing close to the Huntington Beach Pier, just a few miles south of the first observation.

“What happened this week—and we’re very excited about—is there’s never been a recorded instance of any sea turtle nesting on a California beach,” Aquarium of the Pacific President and CEO Jeff Flocken tells SFGate ’s Olivia Harden. “And we’ve had two confirmed sightings of an olive ridley hauling up onto the beach and nesting—digging a hole.”

“Typically, the most north we know of any olive ridley or any sea turtle that nests are in Mexico, so this is quite a bit farther north for them,” he adds.

The first olive ridley was found by lifeguards, Flocken tells the outlet. Different lifeguards spotted the second turtle at Huntington Beach a few days later, Trevor McDonald, marine safety division chief for the Huntington Beach Fire Department, tells Sara Cardine at the Daily Pilot , published by the Los Angeles Times . Experts initially wondered whether the same turtle graced both locations.

They found clarity after Cali Turner Tomaszewicz , a biologist at NOAA’s Southwest Fisheries Science Center, carried out a photo I.D. analysis, according to another social media post by NOAA Fisheries West Coast. Comparing body shape, numbers and locations of barnacles, and shell scale pattern revealed that the turtles were, indeed, two distinct individuals.

The nesting sites have been fenced off and are being monitored by authorities during their typically 45- to 60-day incubation periods, according to the agency, which urges people to keep their distance to avoid disturbing the eggs. These measures can’t protect the nests from every threat, however.

“The biggest hurdles these developing baby turtles face will be cold temperatures as we get deeper into the fall, and the potential for inundation from the extreme high tides that are common this time of the year,” Jeff Seminoff , a marine ecologist at NOAA’s Southwest Fisheries Science Center, explains in a social media post by the City of Huntington Beach.

Olive ridleys are among the smallest sea turtles on the planet. Adults weigh up to 100 pounds and grow to around 2.5 feet long. They’re also some of the most abundant and widespread sea turtles, primarily inhabiting tropical regions of the Pacific, Indian and Atlantic oceans.

stories.title: Laser maps show native woodland returning across the Cairngorms
stories.summary: A Cambridge-led team used airborne laser scans and careful analysis to map millions of young trees across Cairngorms Connect. More than 5,000 hectares of once-open land now support regenerating native woodland after reduced deer pressure.
stories.summaryLong:
A University of Cambridge–led team analysed airborne LiDAR surveys across a large area of the Cairngorms Connect partnership in the Scottish Highlands. The work produced detailed maps showing that millions of young trees have become established, largely through natural regeneration following landscape-scale deer management.

From aircraft flying hundreds of metres above the ground, laser scanning collected data that an AI-supported analysis pipeline turned into individual-tree maps and heights across hundreds of square kilometres. The study reports that more than 5,000 hectares of previously open land now support young woodland, defined as densities above 100 trees per hectare, with only limited planting where seed sources are scarce.

Point measurements on the ground and comparisons with field surveys by Cairngorms Connect partners were used to check accuracy. Researchers describe the mapping approach as a practical way to track whether restoration targets are being met at landscape scale, and note interest in applying similar methods more widely as Scotland expands national LiDAR coverage.

The university news release summarizes a Journal of Applied Ecology paper on tracking and modelling native woodland expansion with LiDAR.
stories.summaryLongNote: Verified from University of Cambridge news release (~210 words).

stories.title: STRATOS: free software that designs airships from hull to fabric
stories.summary: An MIT-licensed open-source tool called STRATOS helps engineers design lighter-than-air craft—from multilobe hull shapes to cut-ready fabric patterns—without juggling a patchwork of expensive CAD packages.
stories.summaryLong:
Airships and long-duration balloons are drawing fresh interest for cargo, science, and low-energy flight, but designing them has often meant stitching together costly CAD tools, fluid-dynamics solvers, and spreadsheets. A new open-source platform called STRATOS, described in the journal SoftwareX and covered by Scienmag, aims to collapse that pipeline into one accessible program.

Developed by Anantha Hari Arun Pedapudi, Sudarsan D. Naidu, Pranav Mittal and Manikandan Murugaiah, STRATOS is released under the MIT License on GitHub and runs on Python 3.10+ with the SALOME geometry platform. A PySide6 graphical interface walks users from blank-screen sizing and geometry generation through physical evaluation and manufacturing output, including CNC-ready fabric patterns for complex multilobe hulls and fins.

The SoftwareX paper positions STRATOS as the first piece of a broader suite that may later add computational fluid dynamics, finite element analysis, and cost modules. For a niche field where exotic hull shapes have been slow and expensive to prototype, an open tool that speaks to both aerodynamicists and fabric cutters is a practical step toward cheaper conceptual design.

Scienmag’s write-up emphasizes accessibility: conceptual design should not require mastery of half a dozen specialized packages. Early users still need engineering judgment—the project is a design accelerator, not an autopilot—but the open license lowers the barrier for students, startups, and labs exploring lighter-than-air vehicles.
stories.summaryLongNote: Verified from Scienmag’s SoftwareX coverage (~240 words).

stories.title: Pakistan expands a sanctuary for the Indus River dolphin
stories.summary: Pakistan created the Punjnad Indus River Dolphin Sanctuary, linking with an existing Sindh reserve into a continuous protected corridor. A recent abundance study estimated roughly two thousand animals—hopeful progress for a rare freshwater dolphin.
stories.summaryLong:
Between 11 million and 16 million years ago, during the high sea levels of the middle Miocene period, the ancestors of the Indus River dolphin entered the muddy waters of what is the Indus Basin today. Over millennia, they adapted to their new environment through extraordinary evolutionary shifts, developing sophisticated echolocation while gradually losing their eyesight.

Today, these blind mammals, living mostly in Pakistan (with a small population in northwestern India), navigate the river’s shallow, dry-season waters by swimming on their sides. Yet, these evolutionary marvels offer little defense against the modern transformation of their habitat.

That habitat is fragmented by vast networks of dams, human-made canals and irrigation barrages. Consequently, the Indus River dolphin ( Platanista minor ), locally known as the bhulan , has seen its historical range slashed by approximately 80% . The species, which boasted an estimated population of 10,000 in the late 19th century, plummeted to just 617 individuals by 2001 before rebounding to around 2,000 over the next decade. The Indus River dolphin is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List .

In response, Pakistan’s government has officially created the Punjnad Indus River Dolphin Sanctuary in June 2026, safeguarding nearly 200 kilometers (123 miles) of the river in Punjab. This new zone connects with an existing protected area in Sindh province, southeastern Pakistan, that creates a contiguous 400-km (249-mi) stretch of legally protected habitat, offering a critical lifeline to one of the world’s rarest freshwater dolphins.

The timing of this legal protection is of the essence, as a landmark 2025 study published in Endangered Species Research (ESR) documented the Indus River dolphin’s metapopulation to have successfully increased to an estimated 1,987 individuals. This reflects a 19.4% increase between 2011 and 2017, demonstrating that past conservation interventions such as the outlawing of dolphin hunting in the 1970s have yielded tangible results. Nearly 99% of this surviving population is now concentrated in a 690-km (430-mi) stretch of the river between the Chashma barrage in Punjab and Sukkur barrage in Sindh province.

“The Indus River dolphin is endemic to the Indus River system, and the overwhelming majority of the remaining global population occurs in Pakistan, with only a very small remnant population now left in the Beas River in India,” Hamera Aisha, lead author of the 2025 ESR study, told Mongabay by email. “This also means that if these populations were lost from the Indus, there is no comparable population elsewhere that could secure the future of the species.”

“This also gives Pakistan a unique global responsibility for the species,” she said.

Despite the encouraging population growth, conservationists warn that these hard-won gains remain exceptionally fragile, and the dolphins, confined to a fraction of their original habitat, face mounting, multifaceted threats.

stories.title: After 27 years, HALO finishes landmine clearance in Kosovo
stories.summary: The HALO Trust concluded its humanitarian demining programme in Kosovo nearly three decades after the 1998–1999 war. Cleared land has helped communities rebuild homes, farms, roads, and everyday life.
stories.summaryLong:
The HALO Trust announced the conclusion of its humanitarian landmine-clearance programme in Kosovo after 27 years. HALO’s account describes arriving after the 1998–1999 conflict, when returning communities faced homes, fields, and infrastructure contaminated by mines and unexploded ordnance.

According to HALO, early clearance of priority danger zones near populated areas, together with risk education and survey work, helped limit later casualties relative to the chaotic immediate postwar period. The charity states that total landmine casualties recorded from 1999 to 2024 were 585, with about three-quarters occurring in 1999–2000 before comprehensive programmes were in place.

HALO links cleared land to later rebuilding of housing, agriculture, roads, airports, and tourism sites, and notes Kosovo’s economy and life expectancy figures as context for postwar recovery—not as sole effects of demining. Programme manager Atholl Stewart is quoted saying impact should be measured in what safe land makes possible over time.

After 27 years, HALO says it is closing operations and handing responsibility for residual contamination to national mine-action authorities, while Kosovar staff carry experience into other programmes.
stories.summaryLongNote: Verified from The HALO Trust news page (~230 words).
